What are Push Notifications?
summary: Learn about push notifications, how they differ from pull notifications, how they work, and the benefits of using push notifications.
body_text: Push notifications are clickable pop-up messages sent from apps or websites directly to a user's device, delivering real-time updates, alerts, and information even when the app isn't open. They use push technology to instantly notify users about important events, enabling immediate engagement without requiring users to actively check for updates. The number of worldwide smartphone users will surpass 7.9 billion by 2028 . That’s no surprise, given that smartphones are becoming both cheaper and more necessary for shopping, dining, transportation, and more. More essential services are moving to smartphones, so consumers have little choice if they want to keep up with the times. Times are changing, and that’s a good thing for businesses. Push notifications (also known as push messages or push alerts) are a powerful marketing tool for acquiring and retaining customers — all they need is a smartphone. Push services, such as Apple's APNs and Google's FCM, use backend infrastructure like google cloud to deliver notifications reliably across platforms and to any mobile device. Push notifications weren’t always around, though. In June 2009, Apple launched the for its smartphones. Soon after, push notifications were developed and adopted on android and ios devices, with mobile operating systems enabling this technology and making real-time communication possible across a wide range of mobile devices. Push messages are an accepted part of downloading smartphone apps. Still, this relatively new frontier has a lot of benefits for brands that strategically leverage the power of push notifications. Push notifications are a key driver of customer engagement on any mobile device, helping brands enhance user experience, retention, and personalized interactions. Check out this guide to learn what push notifications are, why they're so helpful, and best practices to improve your push notifications. What Are Push Notifications? Photo by Jonas Leupe from Unsplash Push notifications are brief, clickable messages sent directly to users’ devices (mobile phones, tablets, or desktops) to deliver timely information, alerts, or updates. Push notifications appear even when users don’t have your app or website open, making them an effective way to reengage with your audience. Push notifications display differently depending on the user’s smartphone and operating system (OS). For example, notification features and behaviors can vary between an iOS device and an Android device. Notification grouping on iOS devices and notification categories on Android help organize alerts, making it easier for users to manage notifications. Device messaging protocols, such as APNS for iOS and Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android, ensure notifications are delivered securely to the user's device. Generally, most smartphones support text-based notifications, while more advanced devices support rich media notifications with images and GIFs. Instead of hoping users will check their crowded email inboxes (they probably won’t), you can send a push notification to engage in a less distracting environment. If you nail your messaging and timing, you’ll improve user engagement and foster brand loyalty at scale. The neat thing about push notifications is that they’re incredibly versatile. Use cases vary by industry: Retail: Direct shoppers back to their abandoned carts with push notifications. These reminders are also great for alerting customers about flash sales or sending order updates. Wellness: Healthcare providers use push notifications to remind patients about their appointments, reducing no-shows. Fitness apps also use these notifications to remind users to log their workouts or get their daily steps in. Banking: Banks send push notifications for fraud alerts, stock updates, or bill reminders News: Some news websites send real-time push notifications that alert readers about breaking news or trending topics. Travel: Flight status updates, hotel booking reminders, and location-based offers are common use cases for push notifications in the hospitality industry. Streaming services: If you have Netflix, you’ve likely received a push notification about your favorite shows or recommended new releases. Many streamers send these notifications with live event reminders, show reminders, and personalized recommendations. When reengaging users, keep in mind that Android users and iOS users may have different opt-in processes and notification experiences, which can affect how and when they receive your messages. The table below provides an overview of how push messages are commonly used in various industries. Industry Example Use Cases Purpose / Benefit Retail Cart abandonment reminders; Flash sale alerts Re-engage shoppers; Drive sales; Increase foot traffic Wellness/Healthcare Appointment reminders; Daily health tips Reduce no-shows; Encourage healthy habits Banking Fraud alerts; Payment due reminders Enhance security; Improve user awareness News Breaking news updates; Trending topic alerts Keep users informed; Drive app traffic Travel Flight status updates; Booking reminders Provide real-time travel information Streaming Services Show reminders; Personalized content suggestions Boost viewer engagement and retention Types of Push Notifications Push notifications have so many applications, but not all push notifications are the same. Push notifications come in several forms, with the primary types being web push notifications, mobile push notifications, and desktop push notifications. Each type differs in terms of delivery platform, technology, and use case: Web push notification: These are the easiest notifications to send. They work through the user’s browser , like Google Chrome or Firefox. Users have to opt in to receive these push notifications. However, there’s no need to create an expensive app to send web notifications , making this a win for businesses on a budget. You can still reach subscribers even when they aren't actively browsing your site Mobile push notification: You need a native app to send mobile push notifications , or you can use a progressive web app to deliver app-like push notifications through the browser. Native apps require not only developing your own app but also persuading users to download the app on their device. The upside is that these notifications access app data, which makes it easier to offer a more personalized experience . Mobile push notifications allow app publishers to send targeted messages to specific users based on their behavior or preferences. They can also use mobile features like geolocation or the phone’s camera. Additionally, mobile push notifications can include rich notifications, such as images, videos, or interactive elements, to enhance user engagement. Desktop notification: It might not sound as exciting as other types of push notifications, but a desktop notification is perfect for targeting business-to-business (B2B) audiences and any user who prefers to use a desktop. Desktop notifications appear on users’ desktops, usually appearing as a desktop popup and display even when the app or browser isn’t open. Web push notifications are great for re-engaging website visitors, mobile push notifications excel in delivering personalized and dynamic content, and desktop push notifications ensure users stay informed about essential updates on their computers. Choosing the right type (or combination) of push notifications will help you reach users at precisely the right time. The table below breaks down the three main types of push notifications and what they’re used for. Type of Push Notification Platform Example Use Case Key Features Web Push Notification Web browsers Re-engaging website visitors No app required; Opt-in needed Mobile Push Notification Mobile apps Cart abandonment reminders Personalized; Uses mobile features (e.g., geolocation, camera); Supports rich notifications Desktop Notification Desktop apps Software updates or meeting reminders Works even when the browser or app isn’t open Push Notifications Versus Email and SMS Push notifications are just one of many potential ways businesses can contact their customers. If you’re already investing in email campaigns and text marketing (SMS) , you might wonder if push notifications are even worth your time. The short answer is yes. Email marketing is the standard in many industries. It supports long-form content and even rich media like images and attachments. It’s pretty easy to automate and forge regular touchpoints with subscribers. Transactional emails , for example, confirm a shopper’s purchase or let a customer know their order has been shipped. However, there's a good chance no one will open — let alone read — the message you toiled so long on. Email open rates, which hover around 32% , are much lower than push notifications and SMS , making them less ideal for urgent messages. SMS is a more personalized way to communicate with users, delivering short messages directly to their smartphones with fewer distractions. Open and response rates are much higher, with a 98% open rate . Still, you have to worry about texting rates and a lack of support for rich media. Push notifications combine the best of email and SMS. They’re urgent, support rich media, and get high response rates. To receive notifications, users must opt in and grant permission, especially on mobile devices. This opt-in process ensures that only engaged users, particularly mobile users, are targeted, allowing businesses to reach people on their smartphones with immediate, relevant updates that are more likely to be seen than emails. In many cases, response rates are as high as 90% , giving SMS a run for its money. The good news is that you don’t have to choose between them — email, SMS, and push notifications all have a place in your outreach efforts. It’s all about knowing when to leverage each option for maximum engagement. The table below provides a comparison of push notifications, email notifications, and SMS messages. Feature Push Notifications Email Notifications SMS Messages Open rate Up to 90% ~32% 98% Supports rich media Yes Yes Limited Message length Short Long Short Cost considerations Typically free (services may have fees) Low to moderate Can incur per-message costs Urgency of delivery High Moderate High Mobile Push Notifications Mobile push notifications are a powerful way for businesses to connect directly with users on their smartphones and tablets. These notifications appear on users’ devices even when the app isn’t open, making them an essential tool for boosting user engagement and retention. With mobile push notifications, app publishers can send personalized messages, special promotions, and timely updates tailored to specific user segments and behaviors. For example, a retail app might use mobile push notifications to remind users about items left in their shopping cart, or a travel app could send real-time flight updates. Mobile push notifications rely on robust push notification services like Apple Push Notification Service (APNs) for iOS devices and Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) for Android devices. These notification services ensure that messages are delivered quickly and securely to users’ devices, helping businesses stay top-of-mind and drive action. By leveraging mobile push notifications, brands can deliver relevant content at the right moment, encourage users to return to their app, and create a more personalized experience that keeps users engaged over time. How Do Push Notifications Work? Photo by Dan Counsell from Unsplash It’s a bit technical, but push notifications need two things to work: Client application: A client application is where your user receives and interacts with notifications. In this case, it’s a smartphone app or web application. Application server: An application server is the web server where you host the application. You have to send all information in the push notification to the server, which then sends the notification to your subscribers. But that’s just the start. Devices and operating systems differ, so developers must learn how to work with the operating system’s Push Notification Service (OSPNS). iOS and Android operating systems have their own OSPNS that developers use to deliver push notifications . This is how the process works once you get the basics down: Build an application: Once you understand the basics of how the OS works, you need to build an application with OSPNSs enabled that connects with iOS and Android push notifications smartphones. The app publisher is responsible for configuring push notification services and ensuring the app is set up to receive notifications. Register with the push service: To access the respective operating systems' OSPNS, you must register with each OS's push notification software . For Android devices, this often involves using backend infrastructure like Google Cloud, which supports notification delivery through services such as Firebase Cloud Messaging. Grab your API: After registering, you then receive access to the API to communicate with the OSPNS. From there, package the push notification capability in the code for the client application and the instance on the app server. User installation: Once the end-user installs the app, the app and device register with OSPNS and generate a unique ID . Users can manage notification permissions and preferences through their device settings, allowing them to control how and when they receive notifications. You can use this to tailor services and push notifications to different users. Send the notification: To send a notification, you can create each message manually and push it to the client app or use the OSPNS API to send automated messages. You can also create an elaborate workflow to create tailored messages to individual users according to different parameters. These parameters include user demographics, subscription status, time of the day, usage pattern, location, etc. Device messaging protocols ensure secure and reliable delivery of notifications to user devices. You’ve got a lot of flexibility here — that’s the beauty of push notifications! Implementing Push Notifications Implementing push notifications effectively requires a thoughtful strategy and the right technical setup. App publishers should begin by outlining their push notification strategy—deciding what types of push notifications to send, how often to send them, and which users to target. This planning stage is crucial for ensuring that notifications are relevant and welcomed by users, rather than disruptive. Next, it’s important to set up the necessary infrastructure. This includes integrating a reliable push notification service and configuring an app server to manage and send notifications. App publishers must also ensure they obtain user permission before sending any push notifications, as respecting user preferences is key to building trust and maintaining high engagement rates. Personalization is another best practice when implementing push notifications. Tailoring messages based on user behavior, preferences, or location can significantly improve user engagement. Additionally, limiting the frequency of notifications helps prevent alert fatigue and keeps users interested in receiving updates. By following these best practices and regularly reviewing the performance of their push notification campaigns, app publishers can create a notification service that not only reaches users but also drives meaningful engagement and long-term retention. How to Enable Push Notifications Enabling push notifications is a straightforward process that starts with user consent. When users first launch an app, they are typically prompted to grant permission for the app to send notifications. This can also be managed later through the app’s settings or the device’s notification preferences. Once users opt in, the app is authorized to send notifications directly to their device. App publishers use push notification services like Apple Push Notification Service (APNs) for iOS devices and Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) for Android devices to manage and deliver notifications. These services provide the necessary APIs and SDKs to send notifications efficiently and securely to users on both platforms. Cloud providers also offer higher-level services like AWS Pinpoint that add segmentation and campaign management on top of these push delivery systems. By enabling push notifications, users can receive timely and relevant updates—such as breaking news, order confirmations, or personalized offers—right on their mobile devices. For app publishers, enabling push notifications is a powerful way to send notifications that drive user engagement, encourage app usage, and keep users informed about important updates. Benefits of Push Notifications Did you know that people have an average of over 80 apps installed on their smartphones? That’s a lot, but get this: people only interact with an average of nine apps daily and 30 apps monthly. That leaves dozens of unused apps on their phones. You certainly don’t want your app to fall by the wayside, and that’s where push notifications come in. They’re a powerful tool for engaging in permission-based marketing , especially in an era of crowded social media feeds and pricey pay-per-click (PPC) ads. Push notifications are also a key tool for marketing campaigns targeting mobile users, helping businesses reach their audience directly on their smartphones. If you aren’t sold on push notifications yet, just consider all of the benefits: Re-engage current subscribers: People who downloaded your app already know about your services, so it’s easier to convince them to re-engage. Use push notifications to grab their attention with exciting offers and irresistible features that persuade them to open your app again. Cut costs : Push notifications are part of your app or website. Unlike SMS, you don’t have to pay per message — it’s already an included feature. It’s incredibly affordable, especially when it supplements pricier strategies like email or SMS. Improve the user experience: The right push notification strategy can give users the information they want when they need it. For example, a football application can send live scores as push notifications so users can view the scores without opening the app and requesting information. Personalize your messaging: It’s actually pretty easy to personalize push notifications. Developers can use parameters like demographic data, location information, and more for each user. Everyone has a unique ID, making it easy to send custom offers or event-based messages to convert these users into paying customers through the power of personalization. Add touchpoints to your sales funnel: Create elaborate sales funnels with the help of web and mobile push notifications. Automate the entire process from the moment the user installs your app. It will continue engaging users over time through messages that boost customer retention and increase customer lifetime value . Whether your goal is to engage, convert, or retain, push notifications have a lot to offer. The only limits are your team’s creativity and marketing acumen — the sky really is the limit. Push Notification Campaigns Push notification campaigns are a strategic way for app publishers to engage users over time with a series of targeted messages. These campaigns can be designed to achieve a variety of goals, such as increasing user engagement, promoting new features, or encouraging users to complete specific actions within the app. To create an effective push notification campaign, app publishers should start by clearly defining their objectives and identifying the target audience. The next step is to design a sequence of push notifications that are personalized, timely, and relevant to users’ interests and behaviors.
